subject: stats
title: Measures of Central Tendency
objectives: Calculate the arithmetic mean, median and mode for ungrouped and grouped data.
Calculate the geometric mean and harmonic mean and identify their appropriate uses.
Calculate quartiles, deciles and percentiles for grouped data.
Select the most appropriate measure of central tendency for a given data set.
study:
A measure of central tendency is a single value summarising the 'centre' of a data set. Four properties are desirable in a good measure: it should be rigidly defined (no room for personal interpretation), based on all observations, capable of further mathematical treatment, and resistant to extreme values.

Key termArithmetic Mean — the sum of all values divided by the number of values. Ungrouped: x̄ = Σx / n. Grouped: x̄ = Σfx / Σf, using class marks. For grouped data with equal class widths, the Assumed Mean (coding) method simplifies the calculation: x̄ = A + (Σfd / Σf) × c, where the deviation d = (x − A)/c.

The mean uses every value and is suitable for further statistical treatment, but it is unduly affected by extreme values (outliers) — a real weakness. The median is the value dividing an ordered data set into two equal halves: for ungrouped data with an odd n, it sits at position (n+1)/2. For grouped data: M = L + [(n/2 − F)/f] × h, where L is the median class's lower boundary, F is the cumulative frequency of the class before the median class, f is the median class's own frequency, and h is the class width. The median's key merit over the mean is that it is unaffected by extreme outlier values.

The mode is the most frequently occurring value — the only measure suited to purely categorical data (like colours). For grouped data: Mo = L + [Δ₁/(Δ₁+Δ₂)] × h, where Δ₁ is the modal class's frequency minus the frequency of the class before it, and Δ₂ is the modal class's frequency minus the frequency of the class after it. A distribution with one mode is unimodal, two is bimodal, and more than two is multimodal.

Exam tipNever confuse the modal class (the class with the highest frequency) with the median class (the class containing the (n/2)th observation, found from the cumulative frequency column) — they are frequently different classes, and CIPM examiners deliberately construct data sets where this is the case.

Two specialised means exist. The Geometric Mean is the nth root of the product of n values, appropriate for averaging rates of growth and ratios. The Harmonic Mean is the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals of the values, appropriate for averaging rates such as speed. For any positive, non-constant data set: Arithmetic Mean ≥ Geometric Mean ≥ Harmonic Mean.

Quartiles divide an ordered data set into four equal parts (Q1, Q2=Median, Q3); Deciles into ten equal parts (D1...D9); Percentiles into a hundred equal parts (P1...P99) — all calculated using formulas structurally identical to the grouped median formula. Finally, a quick way to estimate a missing measure is the empirical relationship: Mode = 3(Median) − 2(Mean). The sum of deviations of all values from the arithmetic mean, Σ(x − x̄), always equals zero — a defining algebraic property of the mean.
recap:
• 4 desirable properties of a good measure: rigidly defined, based on all observations, capable of further treatment, resistant to extremes.
  • Mean: Σx/n (ungrouped), Σfx/Σf (grouped); affected by outliers.
  • Median: (n+1)/2 position (ungrouped); L + [(n/2−F)/f]×h (grouped); unaffected by outliers.
  • Mode: most frequent value; Mo = L + [Δ1/(Δ1+Δ2)]×h (grouped); the only measure for categorical data.
  • Geometric Mean: nth root of product, for growth rates. Harmonic Mean: reciprocal of average of reciprocals, for rates like speed.
  • AM ≥ GM ≥ HM for positive, non-constant data.
  • Quartiles (4 parts), Deciles (10 parts), Percentiles (100 parts) — same formula structure as the median.
  • Empirical relationship: Mode = 3(Median) − 2(Mean).
  • Modal class = highest frequency; Median class = contains the (n/2)th observation — often different classes.

quiz.q: For ungrouped data, the arithmetic mean is calculated as:
opts: The middle value when arranged in order
quiz.why: The ungrouped mean sums the raw values and divides by their count; Σfx/Σf is the grouped-data version using frequencies.

quiz.q: For grouped data, the arithmetic mean is calculated as:
opts: The nth root of the product of the values
quiz.why: Grouped data uses class frequencies and marks: Σfx/Σf, since individual raw values are no longer available.

quiz.q: In the assumed mean (coding) method, the deviation d is calculated as:
quiz.why: The coding method measures each class mark's deviation from the assumed mean A, scaled down by the class width c.

quiz.q: The median of an ordered data set with an odd number of items, n, is located at position:
quiz.why: With an odd count, the single middle value sits at position (n+1)/2 when the data is arranged in order.

quiz.q: In the grouped median formula M = L + [(n/2 − F)/f] × h, 'F' represents:
opts: The frequency of the median class itself
quiz.why: F is the cumulative frequency up to (but not including) the median class; f is the median class's own frequency.

quiz.q: In the grouped mode formula Mo = L + [Δ₁/(Δ₁+Δ₂)] × h, 'Δ₁' represents:
opts: Frequency of modal class minus frequency of the class after it
The class width of the modal class
Modal class frequency minus the class before it
The total frequency of the distribution
quiz.why: Δ1 compares the modal class to the class immediately preceding it; Δ2 compares it to the class immediately following it.

quiz.q: A key merit of the median over the mean is that the median:
opts: Uses every value in the data set
Cannot be found from an ogive
Is unaffected by extreme outlier values
quiz.why: Because the median depends only on position, not magnitude, extreme values in the data don't distort it the way they distort the mean.

quiz.q: A key demerit of the arithmetic mean is that it:
opts: Cannot be computed for grouped data
quiz.why: Because the mean uses every value's magnitude, a single extreme outlier can pull it substantially away from the data's true centre.

quiz.q: When a distribution has values in categories such as 'red', 'blue' and 'green', the most appropriate measure of central tendency is the:
quiz.why: Categorical (nominal) data cannot be meaningfully averaged or ordered, so only the mode — the most frequent category — applies.

quiz.q: A distribution with more than two modes is described as:
quiz.why: One mode is unimodal, two is bimodal, and more than two is described as multimodal.

quiz.q: The nth root of the product of n values, appropriate for averaging rates of growth, is called the …… mean.
quiz.why: The geometric mean is specifically defined as the nth root of a product, making it suited to growth rates and ratios.

quiz.q: The reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals of the values, appropriate for averaging rates such as speed, is called the …… mean.
quiz.why: The harmonic mean handles rate-type data (like speed) correctly, where the arithmetic mean would overstate the true average.

quiz.q: For any positive, non-constant data set, the correct ordering of the three means is:
opts: The three means cannot be meaningfully compared
Arithmetic Mean ≥ Geometric Mean ≥ Harmonic Mean
Geometric Mean ≥ Arithmetic Mean ≥ Harmonic Mean
Harmonic Mean ≥ Geometric Mean ≥ Arithmetic Mean
quiz.why: This inequality (AM ≥ GM ≥ HM) holds for any positive, non-constant data set, with equality only when all values are identical.

quiz.q: A value that divides an ordered data set into four equal parts is called a:
quiz.why: Quartiles split ordered data into four parts; deciles into ten, and percentiles into a hundred.

quiz.q: The median is equivalent to which positional measure?
quiz.why: The median sits at the 50% mark, which is exactly where the second quartile (Q2) falls.

quiz.q: Properties desirable in a good measure of central tendency include all of the following, EXCEPT that it should be:
quiz.why: A good measure should leave no room for personal interpretation — being rigidly defined is the opposite of being determined subjectively.

quiz.q: The empirical relationship linking mode, median and mean is expressed as:
quiz.why: This empirical relationship lets you estimate any one of the three measures if the other two are known, for moderately skewed distributions.

quiz.q: The modal class, as distinguished from the median class, is defined as:
opts: The class with the highest frequency
The class with the lowest frequency
The first class in the distribution
quiz.why: The modal class is identified purely by frequency count, while the median class is located using cumulative frequency.

quiz.q: The median class, as distinguished from the modal class, is defined as:
opts: The class with the single highest frequency count
The last class in the distribution
The class containing the (n/2)th observation via cumulative frequency
The class with the lowest frequency
quiz.why: The median class is found by tracking cumulative frequency until it passes n/2, unlike the modal class which just has the largest single frequency.

quiz.q: The sum of deviations of all values from the arithmetic mean, Σ(x − x̄), always equals:
quiz.why: This is a defining algebraic property of the arithmetic mean: positive and negative deviations from it always cancel out exactly.

cards.front: 4 properties of a good central tendency measure
cards.back: Rigidly defined, based on all observations, capable of further mathematical treatment, resistant to extreme values.
x-bar = Sum(fx) / Sum(f), using class marks and their frequencies.
M = L + [(n/2 - F)/f] x h, where L=lower boundary of median class, F=cumulative frequency before it, f=its frequency, h=class width.
Mo = L + [Delta1/(Delta1+Delta2)] x h, comparing the modal class's frequency to its neighbours.
Averaging rates of growth and ratios; the nth root of the product of n values.
Averaging rates such as speed; the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals.
Arithmetic Mean >= Geometric Mean >= Harmonic Mean, for any positive, non-constant data set.
